title: The Castles of Burgundy
description:
Turn a small estate into a thriving domain by drafting and placing hexagonal tiles. Each round gives you two dice to work with. Their values help determine which tiles you can take and where you can place them. Workers let you adjust a roll, while buildings, castles, ships, and other tiles provide different benefits when placed. Completing regions earns points.

You can also use dice to ship goods or collect workers. Ships can improve your position in turn order, which matters when the next phase brings a fresh set of tiles to the board. Silver gives you another option through the market, letting you pick up a tile outside your two regular dice actions.

A good turn can set off a chain: place a castle, use its extra action to place another tile, and finish a region in the process. You are constantly deciding whether to take the perfect tile now or spend an action preparing a bigger turn later.

title: Terraforming Mars
description:
Run a corporation competing to make Mars habitable. Buy project cards and spend resources to build infrastructure, improve production, and raise the planet’s temperature, oxygen level, and ocean coverage. Terraforming earns points and helps increase income, while many projects create their own scoring opportunities. The game ends once the three global targets are met.

Generations give you repeated chances to turn production into building materials, energy, or money. On the shared map, placing greenery beside a city can affect endgame scoring, while milestones and awards give the table other things to race for. Your corporation’s starting advantages can point you toward a strategy without locking you into it.

The fun is in getting a long-term plan to pay off just in time. A card you buy early might only become playable once the planet warms, while a production upgrade can be brilliant early and almost worthless late. Your rivals can accelerate the ending before your best projects are ready.

title: Cosmic Encounter
description:
Lead an alien species trying to establish five colonies outside its home system. Each encounter sends an attacker’s ships toward another player’s planet. Both sides can recruit allies and choose cards to attack or negotiate, and each species has a power that can bend the rules of the encounter. More than one player can win together.

An encounter can end in a negotiated deal, so committing ships doesn’t automatically mean preparing for a fight. Ask what an ally stands to gain before you invite them. Helping someone earn their fifth colony can be a winning move if the same encounter gives you your own fifth.

Any alliance can become a problem next turn. Help a rival now and they might give you a colony, or they might get close enough to win that everyone else turns on you. The table talk and odd combinations of alien powers make a seemingly straightforward battle delightfully hard to predict.

title: Clank! Catacombs
description:
The catacombs of the skeletal dragon Umbrok Vessna are mysterious and dangerous. Portals transport you all around the dungeon depths. Wayshrines offer vast riches to intrepid explorers. Prisoners are counting on you to free them. Ghosts, once disturbed, may haunt you to death. Despite all that, it's time to leave the board behind with Clank! Catacombs, a standalone deck-building adventure.

Each trip into the catacombs is unique since you lay tiles to create the dungeon. You can play using only the all-new dungeon deck, or you can include cards from previous Clank! expansions.

Find your fortune (and escape the dragon!) in Clank! Catacombs.

title: 7 Wonders
description:
Lead an ancient city through three ages. Everyone selects a card from their hand at the same time, then passes the rest to a neighbor. Build production, trade, science, or military cards as you go, or use a card to complete a stage of your wonder. You can also buy resources from neighboring cities to pay for a building.

Military strength is compared with your immediate neighbors at the end of each age. Science rewards combinations of symbols, while other cards give discounts, produce resources, or score directly. Since the direction of passing changes between ages, a neighbor who fed you useful cards earlier might be the one you’re trying to stay ahead of later.

Each draft asks you to read the table. Do you take the card that completes your set, pick up a resource that will make future cards affordable, or keep a dangerous card away from your neighbor? The simultaneous choices keep the game moving even with a large group.

title: Point Salad
description:
Point Salad is a fast and fun card drafting game for the whole family. There are over 100 ways to score points. Players may use a variety of strategies and every game of Point Salad is unique!

Cards come in six different types of veggies, and the back of each card has a different scoring method. So for instance, one scoring method may award 2 points for every carrot you have, but deduct a point for every onion. By drafting combinations of veggies and point cards that work for your strategy, you can amass the most points and win.

title: Burgle Bros.
description:
Burgle Bros. is a cooperative game. Players are unique members of a crew trying to pull off a robbery of a highly secure building — without getting caught.

The building has three floors (4x4 tiles), each with its own safe to crack. Players start on the first floor and have to escape to their helicopter waiting on the roof.

Players each have three stealth tokens. Whenever they are on the same tile with a guard, they lose one. If any player is caught without a stealth token, the game is over. If players can open all three safes, and escape through the stairs to the roof they win.

title: 7 Wonders Duel
description:
Build a civilization across three ages in a duel for two players. Take exposed cards from a shared display to develop your economy, collect scientific symbols, advance your military, or construct wonders. Every card you remove can uncover an option for your rival. You can win outright through military or scientific supremacy, or earn the most points if both civilizations survive to the end.

A revealed card has other uses if you can’t afford to build it: trade it for coins or tuck it under one of your wonders. Only seven wonders can be completed between the two of you. Your military position and the different scientific symbols you collect give each player something to watch beyond the score.

The fun is in the timing. A card that does little for you may be worth taking to block your opponent, and a wonder that grants another turn can let you uncover a prize and take it before they can.

title: Vaalbara
description:
Lead a clan competing for territory over nine rounds. Everyone has the same set of character cards and secretly chooses one to play. The characters resolve in initiative order, letting you use your chosen ability and claim one of the available territories. Different kinds of territory reward different patterns, from matching types to assembling a varied collection.

Everyone begins with the same twelve characters, so initiative and powers are familiar even when the territories change. Territories can favor collecting several of a type, forming pairs, or deliberately diversifying. You have only nine rounds to make those plans pay, which makes a missed draft pick matter more as the end approaches.

The tricky part is deciding how much you care about going first. A quick character can secure the exact territory you want, while a slower one might offer a stronger effect if your rivals leave you the right options. Knowing that everyone has access to the same powers makes each reveal a small bluff.

title: Citadels
description:
Build the most valuable city by collecting gold and constructing districts. Each round, players secretly draft characters that act in a fixed order and grant different powers. One might bring in money, another help you build faster, and others let you interfere with a rival. Your character changes each round, even as your city grows in front of everyone.

You can use your turn to take gold or draw district cards before building. The roles can change the value of those choices: the Thief targets a character, for instance, so it pays to work out which role a wealthy player is likely to pick. A varied city can also be worth extra points at the end.

A strong board can make your intentions obvious. If you’re sitting on a pile of gold, rivals may guess which role you want and target it. The best rounds are often the ones where you take a less obvious character and make your opponents’ well-laid plans miss.

title: Star Wars: The Deckbuilding Game
description:
Choose the Rebel Alliance or the Galactic Empire and build a deck capable of destroying three enemy bases. Spend resources to recruit units and ships from a shared market, attack with the cards you draw, and push the balance of the Force toward your side to unlock bonuses. When a base falls, its owner chooses a replacement with a different ability.

The market contains cards for both factions as well as neutral recruits. Capital ships can stay in front of your base to absorb hits, so a large attack may have to clear a screen of ships before it can damage the base. That makes building a defense an active part of the duel.

The market is part of the fight. You can attack certain opposing cards before your rival recruits them, so a turn spent denying them a powerful unit can matter as much as a strike on their base.

title: Scarface 1920
description:
Lead a Prohibition-era gang trying to turn a foothold in Chicago into a criminal empire. Recruit associates to improve your deck, send thugs into the city, and use your connections to secure deals, move liquor, and build up your headquarters. Your boss gives your gang its own strengths, which can shape how you make money and expand.

Your crew’s jobs range from recruiting new people to making deals and bribing officials. Upgrading the headquarters helps develop your operation, while Eliot Ness and the federal agents give everyone a common problem. A gang’s leader can make one line of business especially attractive, but who controls the streets will influence which opportunities you can actually use.

The deckbuilding and worker placement come together when the cards you’ve recruited open up a move on the map. Territory is contested, and rivals and law enforcement can upend a plan that looked safe a turn ago. Look for ways to grow without leaving your operation exposed.

title: Codex Naturalis
description:
Build an illustrated record of forest life by placing cards over the corners of pages already in your manuscript. Each placement changes the resources you have available: an insect you cover to make room for a card may be exactly what you need to play a valuable gold card later. After placing a page, draw another to keep your options open.

You can play a card face down when you need more room to build. That side offers four usable corners and a resource, giving you flexibility at the cost of immediate points. Reaching 20 points signals the final turns, before everyone scores their objective cards.

The satisfying part is watching a small arrangement turn into an intricate tableau. Common and secret objectives reward particular layouts and combinations, so where you put a card can matter as much as what it depicts.

Explore new destinations, with the opportunity to trade with those places and get more gains or reputation.

title: The Crew: Mission Deep Sea
description:
Work together on a deep-sea expedition where each mission is a new trick-taking puzzle. Follow the suit led when you can, and use your strongest cards only when they help the crew meet its assignments. One diver might need to win a particular card while another has to avoid taking the wrong trick. Everyone has to succeed for the mission to pass.

A mission may assign several goals at once, and the same hand can be easy or tricky depending on who takes which task. It helps to think about who can lead the next trick, how long their suit might last, and whether they can regain the lead in time to finish an assignment.

Communication is limited, so the order in which you play can tell your teammates more than a conversation would. The best moments come when a seemingly odd move makes sense two tricks later and the entire plan clicks into place.

title: Spies, Lies & Supplies
description:
In this standalone sequel to Air, Land & Sea, two players contest Intelligence, Diplomacy, and Economics instead of the original game's Air, Land, and Sea. Each battle starts with six cards per player and no further draws. You take turns playing one card at a time. If both hands are emptied, compare the total strength on each side of each theater. Whoever controls more theaters wins the battle. The first player to reach 12 victory points wins the game.

Play a card face up to use its printed strength and any tactical ability. Normally it must go into its matching theater. Played face down, it can go into any theater, but contributes only 2 strength and its ability is inactive.

On your turn you can withdraw instead of playing a card. Your opponent wins the battle, but the points they earn depend on how many cards you still hold. Leaving early can keep their score low. Staying in gives you another chance to turn the battle around.

title: Deep Regrets
description:
Head out to sea with a handful of tackle dice and decide how far you’re willing to push your luck. The shadows hint at what’s below, but you only find out what you’re dealing with when you turn a card over. Spend dice to land your catch, or return to port to sell fish, stock up, and recover before heading out again.

The shoals are arranged at three depths, so you can weigh a deeper, less predictable catch against the tackle you have left. Some catches change the situation as soon as they’re revealed or landed. Back on shore, choosing which fish to sell, eat, or mount is another way to stretch a good haul.

The stranger your catch, the more Regrets you can accumulate. They can give you access to more dice and make disturbing catches more valuable, but carrying too many can cost you at the end. Every trip invites one more deeply questionable cast.

title: Solar Titans
description:
Take command of a capital ship in the Orion Centauri system and prepare for battle with opposing vessels.

Solar Titans combines deckbuilding and tableau mechanics, letting you design your capital ship card-by-card. Customize your ship layout to determine its combat capabilities and vulnerabilities. Deploy crew cards from your hand to fire your ship weapons, modify your ship, or buy upgrades from a dynamic market. Take down your opponent's command deck to win!

With six distinct game modes, Solar Titans offers tense solo and co-op boss battles against powerful AI ships, and competitive duels for up to 4 players — including an epic 2v2 format with massive titan-class vessels.

The Definitive Edition adds 16 new market cards with all-new strategic plays, rebalanced solo mode with an improved rulebook, and an upgraded box and custom insert for smoother play and storage.

title: Love Letter
description:
All of the eligible young men (and many of the not-so-young) seek to woo the princess of Tempest. Unfortunately, she has locked herself in the palace, and you must rely on others to take your romantic letters to her. Will yours reach her first?

Love Letter is a game of risk, deduction, and luck for 2–4 players. Your goal is to get your love letter into Princess Annette's hands while deflecting the letters from competing suitors. From a deck with only sixteen cards, each player starts with only one card in hand; one card is removed from play. On a turn, you draw one card, and play one card, trying to expose others and knock them from the game. Powerful cards lead to early gains, but make you a target. Rely on weaker cards for too long, however, and your letter may be tossed in the fire!

title: Puerto Rico 1897
description:
Develop an economy by growing crops, producing goods, and turning them into money or victory points. Each player chooses a role that gives everyone a chance to act, with a privilege for the person who picked it. Build up your town, sell goods to the trading house, or ship goods for points as opportunities open up.

Production only pays off if you have somewhere to send what you make. Selling goods helps finance buildings that improve future turns, while shipping converts goods into points. Roles left unchosen gain money, which can make an otherwise unappealing action worth taking when the next player has a choice.

The game comes alive when you choose a role just before your rivals are ready for it. Shipping at the right time can fill valuable cargo space, while a well-timed build can turn money into an advantage for the rest of the game. Your economy depends as much on timing as on what you produce.

title: Agricola
description:
Start with a small household and build a working farm. Each family member takes one action per round, and a space someone has already used is unavailable until next round. Collect materials, plow and sow fields, build rooms, or fence pastures for animals. Harvests provide food and offspring, but you also have to feed everyone.

The action choices grow as new spaces appear. Early turns may go toward collecting wood or preparing an extra room; later turns can turn that work into more actions or a bigger harvest. A quick improvement that solves this harvest’s food shortage can give you time to develop a more reliable plan for the next one.

A larger family means more actions and more mouths to feed. That trade-off makes even a pile of wood feel urgent when someone else wants it too. Occupations and minor improvements give you different ways to solve the food puzzle while building a farm that scores across crops, animals, rooms, and fields.

description:
In the world of Galecrest, sky pirates set sail on the winds in search of adventure, treasure, and glory. As an admiral, you command a vast and varied crew...but so do your rivals sailing other ships in the pirate fleet. Each day the fleet lands on a different island where you'll send a crew member to collect your share of the loot, hoping they'll return to boost your growing group of characters.

Libertalia was originally released in 2012. Ten years later, Libertalia: Winds of Galecrest celebrates the foundations of the original design with a revised and expanded edition that includes all-new art, 40 characters per player, a reputation system to resolve ties, deluxe loot tokens, a robust solo mode, and much more.

Enter the arena of legends with Final Titan — a Draft Battler where the greatest heroes of all time clash in a fight for supremacy! Who will prove themselves as the "Greatest of All Time" and claim the title of the champion?

In this competitive game, players recruit legendary champions from across time, myth, and fantasy, each with unique abilities, stats, and powers. Once recruited, your champions are thrown into the arena, where they'll face off in intense dice duels.

Choose your matchups wisely, support your heroes with power-up cards, and outwit your opponents.

The last champion standing is crowned the final titan, and the player controlling them is victorious!

title: Grimcoven
description:
Join a coven of hunters and face a boss in a dark Victorian arena. Each hunter has a different development tree, and the group combines dice, abilities, and positioning to build up attacks and respond to what the boss does. Choose an encounter and develop your hunter during the fight rather than working through a fixed story campaign.

Dice allocation connects the small decisions to the big attacks. You might spend dice moving into range, trigger an ability that gives you more options, and use the rest to finish a combo. Lament fuels your growth, but accumulating too much can turn a hunter into the very kind of creature the coven came to fight.

The payoff is turning a few modest actions into a decisive team play. One hunter can set up a position or gather the resources they need, while another uses an opening to land an attack. Different bosses and arenas change what the group has to solve together.

Long Dark Sea is an exploration and adventure card game, where deck-building and resource management are its main mechanics.

Play solo or cooperatively with up to 4 players through an interactive board designed from a modular system that allows customization for each game.

Set in a bespoke science fiction universe, embark on adventures in the quest for ancient relics of great power through a campaign mode that divides each scenario into three distinct acts.

The use of the innovative system allows you to explore, battle, and obtain resources during raid cycles to later enhance your character during supply cycles.

Will you survive until the third act, face the final Nemesis, and escape with your life while claiming the loot?

description:
Leave your nobility at the door in this lighthearted game of hilarious backstabbery! Use any tool to find Excalibur and keep it safe in your “virtuous” hands.

Excalibur is a party game filled with bluffing and subterfuge. Draw tiles from Avalon to find Excalibur, then use the powers of Arthurian legends to keep it safe from the other would-be kings 'round the table!

During each round, players simultaneously draw chips from the 3 regions of Avalon on the table and then reveal them one by one, resolving their effects and discarding them. The game ends when a region of Avalon has no more chips. A player must hold the Excalibur chip to win, otherwise everyone loses.

title: Lands of Evershade
description:
Create a character with a background, class, and personal secrets, then set out across Evershade without a game master. Choose the stories you want to explore and make decisions together as encounters unfold. Character creation shapes the options the story offers you, while combat brings the party onto a tactical map where positioning, abilities, and dice matter.

You can choose standalone story modules and link them into a campaign, letting the group decide which parts of the world to visit. A background or hidden personal goal can give someone a reason to follow a lead that the rest of the party might overlook. In combat, enemies react to what the group does.

Two characters can come away from the same encounter with different reasons to care about what happened. The appeal is having room to play a role and uncover personal story threads while still getting a cooperative fight where everyone has a practical job to do.

title: Point City
description:
From the team that brought you the smash hit Point Salad, Point City is a card-drafting, engine-building game with more than 150 unique building cards, giving you the opportunity to create a completely different city each time you play!

The rules are simple: Take two adjacent cards from the dynamic city grid and add them to your expanding city. Use your resource cards and bonuses to construct building cards that require specific combinations. Build special civic structures to multiply your city's points and be the top urban planner!

Point City takes the same simple concept of drafting cards and building the best combinations, then adds new layers of resource management and engine building to the mix — making the game easy to learn, but challenging for everyone!

title: Catan (base)
description:
Settle an island by building roads, founding settlements, and upgrading them to cities. On each turn, a dice roll determines which terrain produces resources, and anyone with a neighboring settlement or city can collect. Use wood, brick, grain, wool, and ore to expand, trade with the other players, or buy development cards. The first player to ten victory points wins.

The island is built from numbered terrain tiles, so the starting layout changes where good roads and settlements might go. Rolling a seven moves the robber, which blocks production on its new tile and can let the active player steal a resource. The longest road and largest army give you additional ways to score.

Even a strong starting position rarely provides everything you need. You may have the grain someone wants just as they get the brick you’re missing, or a rival might build on the intersection you were racing toward. Trading and timing make the map feel different every game.

Gear up for a thrilling adventure to recover a legendary flying machine buried deep in the ruins of an ancient desert city. You'll need to coordinate with your teammates and use every available resource if you hope to survive the scorching heat and relentless sandstorm. Find the flying machine and escape before you all become permanent artifacts of the forbidden desert!

While featuring co-operative gameplay similar to Forbidden Island, Forbidden Desert is a fresh, new game based around an innovative set of mechanisms such as an ever-shifting board, individual resource management, and a unique method for locating the flying machine parts.

title: Ticket to Ride
description:
Build a railway network across North America and score for the routes you claim and the cities you connect. On your turn, draw train cards, spend a matching set to claim a route, or draw new destination tickets. Completed tickets are worth points, while unfinished ones count against you. Longer routes and the longest continuous path can earn additional points.

The rules are quick to teach because each turn is a single decision. The challenge comes from juggling tickets that can share tracks and drawing the right train colors before key connections disappear. New tickets can be a good late gamble if your existing network already covers the cities on them.

The tension is whether to wait for a better hand or build now to secure a bottleneck. An opponent doesn’t have to know your destination to cut you off. Sometimes a small connection you claim early saves you a long and expensive detour later.

title: FlipToons
description:
Build a cast of cartoon actors and see what happens when six of them audition together. Every round you flip cards into a two-by-three grid, trigger their abilities, and count the Fame they generate. Spend Fame to recruit new performers or dismiss ones who keep spoiling a scene. Once someone reaches the Fame threshold, the game heads into a final audition.

Some talents trigger as soon as a card is revealed, while others care about which other actors appear in the grid. The first cast to reach 30 Fame earns the Critic’s Choice bonus and starts the endgame. Everyone then gets one last chance to put their strongest lineup on screen.

The puzzle is building a deck that puts the right actors next to each other often enough to matter. A performer who looks mediocre on their own might make the entire cast shine in one particular seat. The final flip gives everyone one last shot at a breakout performance.

description:

As a tile-laying artist, you have been challenged to embellish the walls of the Royal Palace of Evora.

In the game Azul, players take turns drafting colored tiles from suppliers to their player board. Later in the round, players score points based on how they've placed their tiles to decorate the palace. Extra points are scored for specific patterns and completing sets; wasted supplies harm the player's score. The player with the most points at the end of the game wins.

title: There and Back Again
description:
Follow Bilbo’s journey through eight chapters, each with its own map and objective. Players draft dice from a shared roll and mark their choices in their own adventure books. A die might let you extend a route, collect resources, or solve a problem specific to the chapter, from escaping trolls to facing Smaug.

The dry-erase book gives each chapter a different set of marks to make. You might chart a route around danger in one scene and use your dice to tackle a riddle in the next. A solo mode and adjustable difficulty let you replay the journey with a different level of challenge.

The book changes the puzzle as the story moves forward, so a good choice in one chapter may do very little in the next. Taking a die can secure the symbol you need while leaving someone else with an awkward option. There’s a satisfying balance between drawing the path you want and making the best of the dice you get.

title: Lord of the Rings Trick-Taking Game
description:
Relive the first part of the Fellowship’s journey as a cooperative trick-taking campaign. Each chapter gives characters different conditions to meet before the team can advance. Frodo may need to capture ring cards, while another character wants to avoid winning tricks. Follow suit when you can and work out who ought to take each trick based on the cards already played.

The player dealt the One Ring takes Frodo’s role, while the others choose from the available characters. That choice lets you look at your hand and work out which objective it serves best. Across eighteen chapters, new characters and challenges change the decisions each hand presents.

What feels like a strong hand can be a bad fit for the character you take. As new characters and challenges enter the story, the same deck asks different questions. A chapter can turn on the moment you realize a teammate was setting you up to win a specific card.

A race ends once two racers have crossed the finish line — with, generally, only these two players receiving points.

title: Goats and Goblins
description:
Lead a party of goblins into a cave full of runaway goats and tempting treasure. Invite other players to come along, then decide how far to press the expedition as you reveal cards. A successful trip lets the explorers divide the haul, but a cave-in can deliver rewards to the goblins who stayed outside. Cards in hand can help or sabotage an expedition.

Cards can be useful during expeditions, but gold on the cards you still hold is what counts at the end. Spending a helpful card now can rescue a haul, while keeping it may make your final score stronger. The dwindling cave deck tells everyone when they’re running out of chances.

Joining the expedition gives you a say in the adventure, while staying behind makes failure look very appealing. The best part is watching a cautious group talk itself into going just a little deeper when everyone knows the odds are getting worse.

title: Inis
description:
Stake your claim to the crown in a Celtic land by spreading your clans, gathering around sanctuaries, or leading territories where rival clans are present. Each season you draft a small hand of action cards, then spend them to move clans, settle new lands, or build up your position. Territorial leadership and epic tales can give you extra options.

At the Assembly, the group works out which clans lead the territories, and those leaders can get cards tied to particular places. Unplayed action cards don’t carry into the next season, but epic tales can be held for later. Deeds can bring you closer to a victory condition, so counting pieces alone can underestimate a rival’s position.

The three paths to victory overlap in ways that make other players’ plans matter. A rival’s clan can help you meet a leadership condition even while it threatens your position. A well-timed pass can also persuade others to spend their best cards while you wait for the moment to declare your claim.

title: Spirit Island
description:
Play as spirits protecting an island and its people from an expanding invasion. Choose how to grow, spend energy on power cards, and combine elements to unlock additional effects. Fast powers resolve before the invaders act, while slow powers can deal with the board they leave behind. Protect vulnerable lands, help the islanders fight back, and generate fear to weaken the invaders’ resolve.

The invaders move through a predictable cycle: a land they explore can be where they build next turn and ravage the turn after. That gives the team a chance to plan ahead. As fear builds, the victory conditions become easier to meet. Different adversaries adjust the pressure and offer ways to raise the difficulty.

Every spirit solves problems differently. One might push explorers into a land that another can devastate, or shield a village long enough for its inhabitants to strike back. The most satisfying turns come when several small powers fit together and stop a crisis the group couldn’t handle individually.

title: Nemesis
description:
Wake aboard a damaged spaceship and try to get home alive. Explore rooms, search for gear, and spend cards from your character’s deck to move and act. Making noise can attract Intruders. The longer you stay, the more there is to check: the state of the engines, the ship’s destination, and whether the next room is as empty as it looks.

Your crew member determines what you can do well. A scientist has tools for research and computers, while a soldier is better suited to a direct confrontation. Intruders respond to the noise you make, and giving them more time can make them harder to deal with. A task that looks manageable now may be dangerous after another trip across the ship.

Everyone has a private objective, so helping another crew member can be useful without being safe. A player rushing toward an escape pod may know something you don’t. That uncertainty makes a quiet walk down the corridor feel like a major decision.

title: An Infamous Traffic
description:
Build a trading fortune in nineteenth-century Qing China in an economic game about the opium trade and the imperial power that sustained it. Establish routes into the interior, lean on smugglers where access is limited, and compete for commercial opportunities as political conditions shift. British intervention can open routes while increasing the risk of instability that can damage the trade you built.

A successful route is a means to an end. Wealth can buy the trappings that make you respectable back in Britain, from a restored estate to a useful marriage or position. Meanwhile, rivals can take advantage of opportunities you helped create, making it important to distinguish what benefits the trade in general from what benefits you.

The tension comes from depending on a system that every merchant has an incentive to push. You’re trying to turn business success into social advancement while watching what your rivals can exploit. A profitable opening can become a liability before you’ve had time to secure it.

As a puny peasant, your only chance to spark a revolution is to fulfill a bizarre legend: find the creature Shug, and bring it to the fabled Pub...

Wander the freeroam map. Befriend monsters like Selky with a sea shanty. Slay your friends with Sexy Armour, or killer salsa moves.

title: Battlesticks
description:
Battlesticks is a light strategy party card game where players collect, combine, and battle a variety of imaginative sticks, each with unique strengths. Inspired by childhood stick fights, the game blends simple mechanics with tactical decision-making, as players build their collections while disrupting their opponents.

On each turn, players draw, play, or use action cards to gain new sticks, enhance existing ones, or interfere with others. Sticks can be modified or combined to increase their power, creating opportunities for stronger plays and strategic timing. Certain cards can trigger battles, where players compete directly using their best sticks.

The objective of the game is to win stick battles and collect rewards. As the game progresses, players must decide when to commit their strongest combinations and when to hold back. The player with the most rewards at the end of the game wins.

title: Re;MATCH
description:
Pick a fighter and attack by clearing connected marbles of the same color from a shared grid. The colors and size of the groups determine what you can do, while your character’s abilities give you different ways to turn a clear into a combo. Each move also rearranges the grid your opponent gets to work with.

You can clear from only two of the three lanes, so a large group of matching marbles may be out of reach until the board changes. Breaking a health bar costs your opponent a quarter to stay in play. Clearing wild marbles can restore that bar, giving a fighter who’s behind a route back into the contest.

Damage is tracked across three colored health bars. Breaking one takes away an attack color, but its marbles can become wild connectors, creating new threats for the fighter you just hurt. The fun is finding a big move that doesn’t leave an even bigger one for your opponent.

title: Roma XLI
description:
Compete to control Rome after Caesar’s death. Play cards secretly as votes to exile a rival or as legions to protect a contender, or play them openly for immediate actions and lasting upgrades. You can spend gold to play beyond the usual single card on your turn, which makes a well-timed reserve valuable. A permanent upgrade can help over several rounds, but a face-down legion can be more valuable when the exile marker is close to triggering and the votes are likely to land on you.

Deals can keep you safe for a round, but every ally wants to be the last contender standing. You might spend a card protecting someone who promised to vote with you, only to find they used that promise to buy time. The uncertainty makes even a single face-down card feel important.

title: 52 Duels: Fight with Playing Cards
description:
52 Duels is a print and play duelling game set in the fantasy world of 52 Realms: Adventures. Using only a standard poker deck, you’ll launch attacks, block damage, use items, and level up your hero’s unique skills. Whittle down your opponent’s deck first to win, but be careful, they’ll have some tricks of their own up their sleeve.

With an ebb and flow similar to trading card games like Magic: The Gathering or Star Wars: Unlimited, 52 Duels offers an affordable, yet deep battling experience that will keep you coming back to the table to try new plays and strategies. Character skills and abilities are contained on one sheet of paper, and health is tracked by how many cards are left in your deck. There is no cutting or crafting required, and you’ll just need a couple of decks of playing cards to play the game.

title: Grifoni: Blades for Hire
description:
Command a mercenary company in Renaissance Italy. Over a series of acts, make choices in the Book of Adventures, then use worker placement to recruit fighters, equip your band, and assign missions. Your decisions steer you toward Glory or Supremacy, opening different objectives and rewards as you build toward the highest score.

The narrative and management decisions alternate. What happens in the story can influence later events, while recruiting and equipping your mercenaries gives you more ways to meet those challenges. The Kickstarter edition’s solo mode also gives a single captain room to explore the company’s options without competing at a full table.

The story gives your management choices a reason to matter. A job can be attractive because it pays, because it helps your company grow, or because it fits the reputation you’re building. The pleasure is seeing a company you’ve shaped through practical decisions become known for the choices you made along the way.

title: Bio Blitz
description:
Assemble a team of real animals and put their abilities to work. Each turn, choose whether to forage for resources, discover cards, or compete for points. Use what you gather to bring new wildlife into your team and look for abilities that work well together. You can win by reaching 30 points or by being the first to complete a team.

When two animals face off, the players roll and add the animals’ bonuses. A strong enough challenge can remove a rival’s animal and earn points based on its value. Trading and exploring give you additional ways to prepare before committing to your main action, so even a turn that ends in a contest begins with choices about how to set it up.

There’s a tempting choice between building steadily and challenging an opponent directly. A matchup can earn points now, while another animal might unlock a combination you can use turn after turn. The two ways to win keep you watching both the score and the teams developing across the table.

title: High Adventure: Treasure Hunt
description:
Lead a solo expedition into the jungle in search of the Grail. Use a pool of dice to manage the expedition’s efforts as you chart a route across a hex map, gather supplies, and investigate clues. Dangerous terrain, illness, and a prowling beast can drain the strength you need for the rest of the journey.

Each turn represents a day, and the sheets track the map as well as events, camp, and the dig itself. Dice help manage both your crew and what they’re carrying. Deciphering tablets can clarify where to dig, but carrying enough gold back also matters if you want to keep the survivors loyal.

You only get one dig, so the growing evidence has to be weighed against the cost of another day in the jungle. Finding the site is just half the job: you still have to get back to camp alive. Every detour offers a little more certainty and gives you one more thing to survive.

title: Rolling Seas
description:
Explore the wonders of the Alkundic Archipelago in Rolling Seas, a swashbuckling roll-and-write maritime adventure game.

As Captain of your ship, you’ll discover new lands, navigate fierce storms and crashing waves, fight off ferocious sea monsters and roaming bandits, burnishing your reputation in the ports and bays of the archipelago as you go.

At the start of each turn you draw an adventure card to see the encounters you will face. It could be plain sailing, or it could be monsters or even storms. You roll dice for wind and exploration effects, and then choose your action for the turn: sail, explore, or visit a port. The more ports you visit, the greater your reputation… provided you have a tale or shanty of adventure you can recount. The player with the most Reputation at the end of 25 rounds is the winner!

So hoist the anchor and cast off, the Rolling Seas await.

title: Rise of the Oak Dell
description:
Rise of the Oak Dell is a strategic roll & write game in which the player takes on the role of a leader guiding a growing civilization in The Oak Dell. Rules will be translated into several languages, however the game itself is 100% language-independent.

Over the course of 13 rounds, they gather resources, develop technologies, explore new territories, and construct wonders of the world — monumental achievements that reflect the power of their people.

But progress comes at a cost: unexpected enemy attacks can disrupt plans, and an unhappy population may hinder development.

title: Avalon: The Riven Veil
description:
Lead a faction onto the mist-covered island of Avalon and compete for control of its lands. Explore the map, establish settlements, and look for legendary items, mythical beasts, and the Grail. Your faction develops as it spreads across the island, and the settlements you establish contribute to your score at the end of the final season.

You can play over two or three seasons according to the chosen game length. Establishing settlements reveals spots on your faction board that contribute victory points, giving your exploration a purpose beyond finding items. Bonding a beast or hunting for the Grail can offer a different direction as the struggle for ground develops.

There’s always a pull between seeing what lies beyond the next patch of mist and securing what you’ve already found. A promising discovery can give you a new direction, but reaching for it can leave territory open to a rival. That balance gives the Arthurian adventure a competitive edge.

title: DECKO
description:
To win in this surreal deckbuilding game players buy supernatural poker cards, burn cards to thin their decks and bend the rules using a plethora of jokers.

The game is structured like a traditional poker game, players bet chips on their poker hands by raising or calling the bet, or fold to get a free new card. Players also get to permanently remove one card from their deck per hand by doing the burn action. After each hand is played all players that didn't win or fold get to buy new special playing cards and jokers, increasing their chances of winning in later rounds.

As the game progresses players will become increasingly powerful and asymmetric in their abilities. The player who has the most poker chips after twelve rounds wins the game

title: Nemesis: Retaliation
description:
Nemesis: Retaliation is the third installment of the Nemesis horror board game series. Like the first two, it is designed as a standalone game.

This time, players take on the roles of highly trained marines, entering the alien nest with strict orders and the most advanced tools available. But will they be well-prepared enough to face the unrelenting horde that awaits them? In Nemesis: Retaliation, players must survive against overwhelming odds and the possibility of betrayal at every step.

Some of the new mechanics are:
Reworked health system
New character actions
Modular map system with special exploration cards
Item management track
Individual objectives allow for hidden traitors

title: Gang Wars
description:
Run a gang trying to dominate Prohibition-era Chicago. Recruit associates into your deck, then play cards to put thugs on the streets, move liquor, or expand your influence in contested neighborhoods. Complete jobs for ongoing benefits and plan around events and police deployments. When the authorities sweep the city, they can confiscate barrels and send your people to jail.

After four rounds, cash combines with the value of jobs, influence, and cars you have on the streets. Thugs left in prison count against you. Bringing people out of jail can therefore matter even late in the game, when it’s tempting to keep every available action focused on earning one last payout.

A neighborhood can be valuable precisely because it’s risky. You have to decide whether to make a quick sale, reinforce your hold, or move your operation before the next sweep. The fun is making the cards in your hand work with a street map that keeps changing.

title: DAVOS
description:
Welcome to the forum, and to this meeting in particular. It is an honor to sit here with those who represent the big capital in the world through your megalomaniacal investment firms.

Tonight in DAVOS, we are going to play out our activities for the coming 3 years. One by one we will be taking over the world's largest corporations in one of the 4 blocs; In America, Europe, China, or the Global South, infiltrate their governments and increase our influence through… other means. To make the world a better place... naturally!

Corporations don't just generate income. You'll need to make sure to pass favorable bills in parliament. You need to invest your assets strategically, balancing between corporations and politics. And balancing between reaching goals directly, or investing for improving your power position in future years.

Do you crave more? Advance your game via the back room and gain control of institutions. Play together in the collaborative variant, or become dissident and follow an anti-agenda, disrupting other players.

title: Hitman: The Board Game
description:
A 1-4 player competitive board game where success depends on improvisation, creativity, and surgical precision. Travel the world, infiltrate exotic locations, and eliminate high-profile targets - but this time, you won't be alone. Other agents have also been assigned the contract, and they’ll stop at nothing to sabotage your mission and deliver the killing blow. Guns blazing or silent assassin? The choice is yours.

The game is based on the Hitman video game franchise and was developed in collaboration with IO Interactive.

title: Brass: Pittsburgh
description:
From Roxley and Gavan Brown, co-designer of Brass: Birmingham, comes Brass: Pittsburgh, which allows you to re-experience the explosive late 19th-century industrial boom of America's Gilded Age in its northeastern "Steel Belt" region (1865-1913). Players take on the role of a ruthless industrial titan in the age of Cornelius Vanderbilt, Andrew Carnegie, John D. Rockefeller, and Henry Frick as they build sprawling networks of railways, pipelines, steel mills, oil refineries, and more.
Built on Martin Wallace's acclaimed Brass system, this standalone game introduces innovative new mechanisms and content, while maintaining the overall structure and strategic depth for which Brass has become known.

title: The Old King's Crown
description:
Compete for an empty throne by sending followers to contest locations across an overgrown kingdom. Move your Herald openly to show where you’re staking a claim, then commit cards face down to different regions. Once everyone reveals, the clashes yield rewards and opportunities to build influence. Your faction’s abilities give you different ways to turn those contests to your advantage.

Players commit their cards at the same time, so you can’t wait to see what your rivals have sent before deciding how much strength to put in a region. The rewards vary by location. Picking where to fight is just as important as winning the fight, especially when you need influence to finish ahead.

The visible Herald and the hidden cards make it possible to tell two different stories about what you want. A rival may commit their best follower to stop you in one place while you quietly take what you needed elsewhere. Reading those intentions is half the fun.

description:
A once-abandoned asylum now harbors something far worse than its crumbling walls suggest. People are vanishing, eerie chants fill the air, and strange lights flicker in the darkness. The ritual is not yet complete — there is still time to act. As elite B.E.L.O.W. agents, you are the last line of defense against the horrors that should not exist.

With a Lovecraftian theme, B.E.L.O.W.: Asylum is a fully cooperative, one-shot action-horror board game that blends deep strategy with an immersive, ever-evolving narrative. Play as unique, asymmetric characters, each with distinct abilities, as you uncover the truth hidden within the asylum’s haunted corridors. Face off against bizarre and lethal threats, adapt to unpredictable challenges, and master protective rituals to halt the growing evil.

Players must activate 4 artifact seals around the board and finish the ritual to defeat the Monarch. With randomized board tiles, exploration cards and ritual rings, there is great replayaility.

title: The Wandmaker's Apprentice
description:
Craft your legacy or wield the shadows.
The choice is yours.

Following the fallout between master and apprentice, we find the apprentice recessed in the shadows, where the law's light seldom reaches. There, in the dark alleyways, he has set up his own trade, selling wands and other magical objects imbued with wild, untamed magic (and questionable legality). The street lamps flicker with the tension of a town caught between light and darkness. Master and apprentice locked in an unspoken war, each wand sold — a silent challenge to the other’s legacy.

In The Wandmaker's Apprentice, you will take on the role of either:

The Wandmaker — crafting genuine wands from resources such as wood, gems, dragonbone, and stardust.

or

The Apprentice — perfecting the art of persuasion to peddle dark magical objects, while avoiding the Magical Authorities.

This asymmetric 2-player game utilizes unique mechanics and components for each player, combining elements of resource management, end-of-round-bonus building, a twist on set collection, and a clever dice management system.

title: Andromeda's Edge
description:
Build a civilization at the edge of the Andromeda Galaxy. Each turn, either launch a ship to a region or bring your ships home. Send them out to gather resources, visit bases, and compete for a foothold on planets. Returning lets you put your station modules to work, while new developments and progress across several tracks help build your score.

The progress tracks cover science, industry, commerce, civilization, and supremacy. Building developments on planets or adding modules to your station can help you move up them. Some advances matter during the game as well as at final scoring, so where you send a ship can influence both the next return and your longer-term goals.

Each launch is a chance to improve your next return, but occupied regions can bring you into conflict with rivals or raiders. The satisfying moment is bringing your fleet back and chaining a set of station abilities you’ve built yourself. Waiting one more turn can make that payoff bigger or give someone else the position you wanted.

description:
Defend Vigil in a deckbuilder where you recruit heroes, buy constructs, and defeat monsters from a shared row. Build up the resources and attack power in your deck, then turn them into Honor. The player with the most Honor at the end wins. A legendary track lets you unlock abilities, while defeating Remnants can reward you for leaning into particular factions.

Runes and power give you two different ways to use a turn: recruit more cards or deal with monsters in the center row. Heroes cycle through your deck, while constructs can stay in play to support later turns. Advancing on the legendary track gives you another reason to look beyond the immediate Honor value of a card.

The changing row keeps you adapting to opportunities as they appear. A dual-faction card might connect two parts of your deck, or an unexpected monster might give you a better payoff than another recruit. There’s pleasure in watching a few sensible purchases become an engine that feels like your own.

description:
Combine two factions into a deck and try to drain your opponent’s Nexus from 30 energy to zero. Play units, support cards, and events, then commit attackers to a fight. Your attacking units are discarded after the attack, so sending more pressure now comes at the cost of resources you might want for the next exchange.

A match starts by drafting factions from a revealed pool, with the exact setup depending on the mode. Last Dawn and Warnarok give you different factions to mix. Each turn runs from drawing and playing cards to a separate attack step, so you can plan support and defense before deciding how much to commit.

Each faction brings its own tools, and mixing them is where the game opens up. One can supply the setup another needs for a big attack, or help cover a weakness in defense. The exchanges move quickly, which makes it easy to try a new pairing and immediately see how differently it plays.

title: Tend
description:
In Tend, players take on the role of a pioneer working for the Zenith corporation to start a homestead on a new alien world.

Tend is a "flip and write" game where players are each building up their own farm and collecting the greatest selection of goods to send back to Zenith HQ for study. All players will be using the same deck of action cards each round to simultaneously take actions on their own sheets.

As the game progresses new cards will be added to the shared deck, changing what actions are available for the whole table throughout the course of the game.

Players earn victory points for collecting badges, completing season objectives, being the best neighbor, and filling up their Cargo Manifest with goods to send back to Zenith HQ. In the end, the player with the most victory points wins!

title: San Juan
description:
Build a city with a hand of cards that doubles as your spending money. You can construct a building or give up other cards to pay for it. Each player chooses a role that lets everyone take its action, with a bonus for the person who chose it. Production buildings create goods to sell for more cards, while special buildings give you abilities and scoring options.

You can produce goods and then trade them for cards to fund your next building. That can be a good plan if your production buildings are ready, while a player with an efficient set of special buildings may profit more from repeatedly choosing Builder. The game ends when a player has constructed twelve buildings.

A card you want to build may also be the one you need to spend to get going. That makes each new hand interesting, especially when choosing a role could help your rivals as much as it helps you. The best turns turn a modest hand into a lasting advantage.

title: Annulet
description:
Build a kingdom by drafting cards from a shared river. Compete for initiative to get the first choice, then collect lands for scoring sets, use characters to change how those lands score, or take annulets for stones that can buy extra actions. Personal fate cards give you ways to change the pace, while shared tale cards can change the rules for everyone.

Characters are placed on lands, which makes the order of the draft important: a piece that looks ordinary on its own can become valuable once you have the right place to put it. Stones can also contribute at the end, giving you a reason to weigh the value of an extra action against keeping them.

There’s a nice choice between taking points you can see and investing in the freedom to do more later. A character can turn a collection of lands into a stronger scoring plan, and a newly revealed tale can make you reconsider which card in the river matters most.

title: Brass: Birmingham
description:
Build an industrial network in the Midlands across the canal and rail eras. Spend cards and money to establish industries, connect towns, develop stronger tiles, and sell goods. Coal, iron, and beer shape what you can do, and many tiles earn points once their output has been used or sold. Established industries and transport links score at the end of each era.

Scout lets you discard cards to gain wild cards, which can help when your hand doesn’t match the industry or town you want. Beer can be needed to complete sales, so a plan to expand production also needs a way to get goods to buyers. Loans let you act sooner but reduce your income.

The economy is shared, so a rival’s coal or beer can let you make the move you wanted while helping them profit. That creates interesting choices about when to invest in your own supply and when to take advantage of someone else’s. The switch to rail gives you a new chance to capitalize on the network.

title: Brass: Lancashire
description:
Build mills, mines, ironworks, and ports in industrial Lancashire. Use cards to build industries or transport links, upgrade what you can build, sell cotton, and borrow when cash runs short. Canals connect the early economy, then railways take over in the second era. Industries score once they’re established, and links earn points from the places they connect.

The cards in your hand help determine which locations and industries you can build, while developing can remove weaker tiles to make better ones available. Networks and industries score at the end of both eras. Timing a cotton sale or investing in the connections that will still matter after the canal era can shape the rest of your game.

Much of the fun lies in working out who will use what. A rival can consume your coal or iron and help flip your tile, while selling cotton through a port can benefit its owner. Spending less can also move you earlier in the next turn order, letting you pull off two moves before rivals can react.
